title: 2 Samuel 24:18–25
context: Gad tells David to build an altar on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite; Araunah offers the site, oxen, and wood freely, but David insists on paying, saying he will not offer to the LORD what costs him nothing. David builds the altar, offers sacrifices, and the plague stops. Both traditions read this as shared ground, and both note that the site later became the location of Solomon’s temple (2 Chr 3:1).

verses.text: Gad came that day to David and said to him, “Go up, build an altar to the LORD on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Gad tells David to build an altar on Araunah’s threshing floor. Arminian readers note that God provides the way of atonement.

The place of judgment becomes the place of worship.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God directing worship to a specific place.

2 Chronicles 3:1 identifies the site with Mount Moriah, where Solomon’s temple was built.

verses.text: David went up according to the saying of Gad, as the LORD commanded.
verses.arminianNotes:
David goes up as Gad said, “as the LORD commanded.” Arminian readers note David’s obedience.

Repentance leads to obedient action.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the king submitting to God’s word through the prophet without delay.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: obedience follows confession, and worship follows God’s command.

verses.text: Araunah looked out, and saw the king and his servants coming on toward him. Then Araunah went out and bowed himself before the king with his face to the ground.
verses.arminianNotes:
Araunah sees the king coming and bows to the ground. Arminian readers note Araunah’s respect for David.

The Jebusite honors Israel’s king.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see a scene of humility on both sides, as the king comes to a Jebusite’s threshing floor to seek God’s mercy.

Both traditions note that Araunah receives the king with honor.

verses.text: Araunah said, “Why has my lord the king come to his servant?” David said, “To buy your threshing floor, to build an altar to the LORD, that the plague may be stopped from afflicting the people.”
verses.arminianNotes:
David explains he wants to buy the threshing floor to build an altar so that the plague may stop. Arminian readers note the purpose: intercession for the people.

David acts for the nation.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see sacrifice as God’s appointed means to end the plague, with David acting at God’s command (v. 18).

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the altar is built for the people’s sake.

verses.text: Araunah said to David, “Let my lord the king take and offer up what seems good to him. Behold, the cattle for the burnt offering, and the threshing sledges and the yokes of the oxen for the wood.
verses.arminianNotes:
Araunah offers cattle, threshing sledges, and yokes for the offering. Arminian readers note his generosity.

He offers everything needed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see a gracious offer from a foreigner.

Araunah’s willingness contrasts with the solemnity of the moment.

verses.text: All this, O king, does Araunah give to the king.” Araunah said to the king, “May the LORD your God accept you.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Araunah gives all to the king and says, “May the LORD your God accept you.” Arminian readers note his blessing.

He acknowledges Israel’s God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see a foreigner blessing Israel’s king and acknowledging Israel’s God in the moment of judgment.

His words express hope that God will accept David’s offering, which both traditions treat as shared ground.

verses.text: The king said to Araunah, “No, but I will most certainly buy it from you for a price. I will not offer burnt offerings to the LORD my God which cost me nothing.” So David bought the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver.
verses.arminianNotes:
David refuses: “I will not offer burnt offerings to the LORD my God which cost me nothing.” He pays fifty shekels. Arminian readers note the principle that true worship involves cost.

Fifty shekels is the weight named here; 1 Chronicles 21:25 gives a different price for the site.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also see sacrificial worship, which Christians often apply to wholehearted devotion (cf. Rom 12:1), as an application.

The price difference with 1 Chronicles is a textual issue interpreters discuss.

verses.text: David built an altar to the LORD there, and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings. So the LORD was entreated for the land, and the plague was removed from Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
David builds an altar, offers burnt and peace offerings, and the plague stops. Arminian readers note God’s response to sacrifice and prayer.

The book ends with worship and mercy.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see atonement and reconciliation through sacrifice.

Both traditions note that this site became the temple location (2 Chr 3:1), ending the book with hope.
